body.markdown: My grandmother used to say the lemon trees here remember when the villages were smaller, when the terraces stretched unbroken from Monterosso to Riomaggiore. Walking past them on an early morning, you understand what she meant. These aren't the tidy ornamental trees you see in garden centers—these are gnarled, centuries-old sentinels with bark like weathered hands and branches that know exactly how to catch the sea wind without breaking.

The scent hits you before you see them. Not the clean citrus of a supermarket lemon, but something deeper—flowers and fruit at once, mixing with salt air and the green smell of the vines growing nearby. In spring, when the white blossoms open, the entire coastline becomes a kind of church. Bees know it. They arrive in such numbers you can hear them from the path above.

Most tourists walk right past, heading toward the next village, the next photograph. They don't notice the stone shelters built around the trees—wooden frameworks covered in reed mats that locals call paìe. These go up every November to protect the trees through winter. Taking them down again in March is its own ritual, one my uncle still observes, though fewer people do each year.

The lemons themselves hang like lanterns in the shade, impossibly large and aromatic. We use them in everything—pasta, fish, limoncello that never makes it to any shop. When you taste one fresh from the tree, the tartness makes your eyes water, but underneath there's a sweetness no supermarket fruit ever achieves. The difference between swimming in a pool and swimming in the sea.

At sunset, when the light goes copper and the day-trippers have caught their trains, I sometimes sit beneath the oldest tree in my family's terrazza. The fruit glows like it's holding the last of the sun. The tree was here before I was born, before my grandmother was born. It'll be here after, roots gripping the hillside, branches reaching toward Africa, patient as stone.
